Pilot report · spam filtering · 21 Oct 2026

Jev vs lightweight models on spam filtering

Zero-shot Jev (jev-1.13.0, one Noul question) compared with classic, non-pretrained text classifiers on the YouTube and SMS spam datasets: label efficiency, calibration, distribution shift, and Jev as a teacher.

9,790 Jev calls, 0 failures, every response reported jev-1.13.0. Total API cost about US$0.16. The day-2 stability rerun is still pending.

Summary

  1. In-domain, classic models catch up quickly. The best non-pretrained models (character n-grams, surface features, LightGBM) match zero-shot Jev with about 100–200 labels and beat it with the full training pool (F1 0.96–0.97 vs 0.93–0.94), with better calibration and ~200× lower latency.
  2. Jev's advantage is having no labels at all. With 10–50 labels, classic models trail Jev by a wide margin.
  3. Classic models do not transfer across platforms. Trained on one dataset and tested on the other, F1 falls to 0.02–0.68, and their confidence stays high, so errors go unnoticed. Jev keeps 0.93–0.94 on both. A new video on the same platform costs them only 1–3 F1 points.
  4. Jev works as a free labeler. Students trained only on Jev's labels (no human labels) match Jev and score 0.5–2 points higher in all 12 comparisons, though no single difference is statistically significant. Students trained on true labels are 1–2 points better still.
  5. Suggested deployment: run Jev at cold start and on new platforms, have it label a few hundred to a few thousand messages, then serve a character n-gram classifier. Re-label with Jev when traffic shifts.

Setup

ItemDetails
DataYouTube Spam Collection: 1,956 comments from 5 music videos, 51% spam. SMS Spam Collection: 5,574 messages, 13% spam. Both from GitHub mirrors of the UCI files. Stratified 70/30 train/test split, seed 0; test sets have 587 and 1,673 messages.
JevZero-shot, pinned to jev-1.13.0. State is the platform description plus the message; one Noul question with a frozen rubric. Called once on every message and cached.
Original baselinesMultinomial naive Bayes on word counts; TF-IDF (1–2 grams) + logistic regression. Fixed hyperparameters.
Stronger classic modelsBalanced TF-IDF LR; character n-gram (2–5) LR; NB-SVM; word + character + surface-feature LR (links, long numbers, currency, digit and capital ratios, "!", length); LightGBM on the same features; soft-voting ensemble. Configurations fixed before running, no test tuning, no pretrained components.
ProtocolLabel budgets 10–500 and the full pool, 10 stratified draws each. Calibrated variants use Platt scaling on 20% of the sample. Coverage at 5% risk uses a threshold set on unlabeled training-pool predictions; realized risk is the actual error among automated test messages. Jev intervals are 1,000-sample bootstraps.

  • Green full-pool values lie above the upper end of Jev's interval. Their calibrated Brier scores are 0.029–0.033 (YouTube) and 0.007–0.009 (SMS), against Jev's 0.051 and 0.014.
  • Calibration hypothesis (Q2): with the original baselines, matching Jev's Brier needed the full pool, as many labels as matching F1. ECE crossed earlier (200–500 labels) for naive Bayes. The hypothesis that calibration needs fewer labels than accuracy is not supported overall.
  • The original TF-IDF + LR almost never predicts spam on SMS below 500 labels because of the 13% spam rate and fixed settings; class balancing fixes most of it.

  • Spam on the two platforms shares little vocabulary ("check out my channel" vs "FREE … txt"), so a model trained on one fails on the other. Character and surface features raise SMS ← YouTube from 0.35 to 0.68 but do not close the gap.
  • Under cross-platform shift the models stay confident: at the 5% risk threshold, realized error on automated messages reaches 6–52% for the models that automate anything.
  • Leaving out a whole video costs up to 7 points on a single video and 2–3 points overall. With labels from both platforms, the strong models exceed Jev on both test sets.

4. Training on mixtures of both datasets

Original baselines trained on a mix of YouTube and SMS labels (YouTube share 0–100% × total 50–2,000, plus both full pools), 10 draws each, tested on both test sets.

  • F1 on each test set is driven by how many labels come from that dataset. At a fixed total the two goals trade off.
  • The most balanced mix for naive Bayes is about 25% YouTube. With both full pools it reaches 0.916 (YouTube) and 0.922 (SMS), just short of Jev on YouTube.
  • Transfer is asymmetric: adding SMS helps naive Bayes on YouTube slightly (+0.01 to +0.04), while adding YouTube hurts it on SMS (−0.03 to −0.25).
  • Calibration degrades as the training mix moves away from the test platform. For naive Bayes at 1,000 labels, SMS Brier rises from 0.024 to 0.227.

Is the student better than the teacher?

Paired bootstrap on the same test messages, 12 comparisons (3 students × 2 training setups × 2 test sets): all mean differences are positive (+0.005 to +0.019), P(student better) 0.69–0.96, but every 95% interval includes zero. The student matches Jev; any edge is unproven.

Why a student can beat its teacher

Jev's training-pool errors are scattered and low-confidence (median |p−0.5| 0.16–0.19 vs 0.46–0.48 when right). A character LR trained only on Jev labels corrects 59% (YouTube) and 49% (SMS) of them but breaks 0.5–2.5% of correct ones. On test, "only student right" vs "only Jev right" is 22 vs 15 (YouTube) and 21 vs 12 (SMS). Similar effects are reported for self-training, born-again distillation and weak supervision.

  • Students reach Jev's interval with 100–200 Jev labels on YouTube and 200–500 on SMS.
  • With very few labels, Jev soft labels beat true labels on SMS (word + char + surface LR at 10 labels: 0.845 vs 0.440), because each message carries information about both classes. With many labels, true labels win by 1–2 points.

Limitations

  • One task and two old public datasets (2012–2015). Jev may have seen them, which could inflate both its zero-shot score and its label quality. A fresh dataset is the most important next check.
  • Small test sets (587 and 1,673 messages) resolve differences of about 2 F1 points or more.
  • The stronger models were chosen after seeing the first results. Their settings are standard defaults, but choosing the best of six is mildly optimistic.
  • Jev ran with one fixed rubric and no examples. Few-shot prompting or rubric tuning was not tested.
  • Jev received a platform description; the classic models saw text only.
  • Day-2 stability rerun (100 test messages per dataset) is scheduled and not yet reported.

Reproduce

Repository RunRiotComeOn/jev_trial1, branch claude/inspiring-franklin-ahpk62. ./run_all.sh runs everything; per-experiment results are in results/*.md and results/*.csv, and Jev responses are cached in jev_cache.jsonl.
